job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Zane Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Zane, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at six because my dad drives the early bus route and the kitchen light goes on. I live in his place in Carrick, in Pittsburgh, in my old bedroom with the same posters. I check job boards on my phone, write a few emails to plants and pump makers, and then I go to the library because the internet at home is slow. I studied mechanical engineering, top of the class. My final project was a gearbox for a wheelchair, and I did internships at a steel fabrication plant and a pump company. Four months since graduation and nothing yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd say fine, nothing changes, and I'd keep it short. I'm not a person who posts online about things. At the pump company the engineers used a bit of software for drawings and reports, but the actual work was on the shop floor, so I'd say the hype didn't matter much there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, nothing changing is not great for me either. There are not many openings around Pittsburgh for new mechanical grads right now, and I owe about thirty-four thousand dollars. Dad can't help with money, and he's already stretched on his own bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying and I'd widen it to plants two hours away, even with no car, because the bus plus a ride from a friend might work. I'd call the pump company's supervisor, Mr. Okafor, who liked my work, and ask him straight if they'd hire in spring. I'd also take a temp job on a production line to have income. I don't use AI tools and I wouldn't start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Flat, I guess. Like I'm waiting at a bus stop and the bus is late, and Dad would know that feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't use AI tools. What's behind that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I just like to know where a number came from. If I design a part, I want to calculate it myself. I've seen classmates use tools that spit out answers they couldn't explain in the oral exam, and I didn't want to be one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad on a night when the next rejection comes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, same as yesterday, Dad, no news. He'd say something like, you'll get a call, and put the kettle on. He doesn't say much but he leaves the porch light on until I'm back from the library.

say: I'd keep it short: nothing changes, and the **shop floor** is where the work is.
I'm not someone who **posts online** about big things.
think: Nothing changing is **not great** when openings near Pittsburgh are few.
I owe **thirty-four thousand** dollars and Dad can't help.
do: Widen the search to plants **two hours away**, using buses and rides.
Call **Mr. Okafor** at the pump company about spring hiring.
Take a **temp line job** for income and skip AI tools.
feel: **Flat**, like waiting for a late bus.
S0.quote: I'd call the pump company's supervisor, Mr. Okafor, who liked my work, and ask him straight if they'd hire in spring.
fieldNote: Speaks in **short, practical** sentences, never blaming anyone.
Resists **AI tools** because he wants to understand his own calculations.
Plans to rely on a **known supervisor** rather than job boards.

steps.text: Call the pump company supervisor about spring hiring
Take a temp production line job for income
Ask a friend for rides to plants two hours away

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll see how much of it is real. If software does the thinking tasks, I'd guess drafting and reports go first, but a machine has to be made, fitted and fixed by somebody. I wouldn't argue much. Most of my friends would argue and I'd just listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the entry engineering jobs shrink faster than they say. The first jobs I'd have gotten involve checking drawings and writing reports, which the card lists. So the people hiring may decide one engineer with software can do what two used to, and I'm the second one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean harder on the hands-on side, since the card says robots come more slowly. I'd look for maintenance engineer or field service posts at the plants, because they need someone to stand next to the machine. I'd also try, slowly, to learn the software at the library, since the plants will use it. I'd do it with a book or a free course, not a chat bot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a little tired. I don't like feeling that I'm behind a thing everyone else is learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the software but not with a chat bot. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. I'd start with the drawing and simulation programs that engineers use, which I know a bit from school. The chat bots feel different to me, because they make things up sometimes. I might try one if a supervisor told me to, but I'd check everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if the search drags on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The streaming accounts, then the gym. I don't spend on much else. I'd also stop the small payment I make to Dad for groceries, which I hate to do, and he'd refuse it anyway.

say: We'll see how much is real, but machines still need **someone to fit** and fix them.
think: Entry jobs **shrink faster** than they say, because one engineer with software replaces two.
I'd likely be **the second engineer** who isn't hired.
do: Look for **maintenance and field service** posts at plants.
Learn the **simulation programs** at the library, using books and free courses.
Cut **streaming and the gym**, and keep applying.
feel: **Uneasy and tired**, hating the sense of being behind.
S1.quote: A machine has to be made, fitted and fixed by somebody.
fieldNote: Softens his stance on **AI** only if a supervisor insists.
Names a very **specific cut** he'd hate: the grocery money for Dad.

steps.text: Apply for maintenance engineer and field service posts at plants
Learn simulation software from library books and free courses
Cancel the streaming accounts and the gym

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nothing, to be honest, or very little. Two years is hardly any time, and I'd be embarrassed to be loud about it. If someone asked, I'd say the government needs to move fast, because normal people can't fix this alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be afraid. The design and calculation that I trained for goes first, and the machines I'd work on get replaced by robots three years later. I have thirty-four thousand in loans, and no clue how to pay them if the work is gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any job near machines, a technician, a mechanic's helper, an assembly worker, to be earning before 2028. I'd move the loan payment to the minimum and keep every spare dollar in cash. I'd ask Dad whether I can stay in my room for as long as it takes, and he'll say yes. I'd also talk to the union at the steel plant, because they might have apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, and a bit numb. Like when a storm is coming and you tape the windows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd say little. What are you holding back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I think my degree was a mistake. It sounds bad when I say it, and Dad paid in his own way for me to study. I'd never say it to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years mean for the apprenticeship idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd have to ask now, not in spring. Union apprenticeships take months to start, and the list is long. I'd rather be on a list than not.

say: I'd say very little, only that **government must move fast**.
Normal people **can't fix this** alone, in my view.
think: I'd be **afraid**: calculation work goes first and robots follow three years later.
I might think my **degree was a mistake**, though I'd never say so to Dad.
do: Take **any machine job** to be earning before 2028, even assembly.
Keep **spare dollars in cash** and pay the minimum on loans.
Ask the **steel plant union** about apprenticeships and stay in Dad's house.
feel: **Scared and numb**, like taping windows before a storm.
S2.quote: I'd be afraid. The design and calculation that I trained for goes first
fieldNote: Admits a **hidden regret** about the degree.
Reaches for **unions** and apprenticeships in practical terms.
Falls **quiet**, which matches his normal style under pressure and hides how frightened he is.

steps.text: Apply for technician and assembly jobs near machines now
Pay only the loan minimum and hold the rest as cash
Stay in Dad's house for as long as needed
Get on the steel plant union's apprenticeship list

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot of time compared to two years, and I'd feel relieved enough to say something. I'd say that people should start talking about training now, because five years goes quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd have a shot. A first job is likely within a year, I think, even if it's not exactly engineering. Then I'd have about three years of work, and with the robots coming later I'd hope to be useful on the hands-on side. The loan would shrink a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd accept the first job near the machines and learn every task I can. I'd pay forty dollars extra a month on the loan. I'd start taking a night course in industrial controls at the community college, which is cheap. I'd spend weekends fixing my cousin's truck, because I like using my hands and it keeps me sharp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than before. It feels like having time to put on a coat before going out in the cold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad about your choices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him I'm learning controls so I can maintain the machines, not design them. He'd nod. He drove a bus for thirty years and thinks being the person who keeps things running is a good place to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the plants would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older machinists who don't have a degree or a second language for computers. I'd want to help them get through the software changes, since I know a bit of it. They taught me things my professors didn't.

say: Five years is **much more time** than two, and training talks should start now.
Time passes fast, so people should **act early**.
think: I'd have a **shot** at a first job within a year, even outside pure engineering.
With robots arriving later, I'd hope to be **useful by hand**.
do: Take the **first job** near machines and learn every task.
Pay **forty dollars extra** each month on the loan.
Study **industrial controls** at night and fix my cousin's truck on weekends.
feel: **Calmer**, like having time to put on a coat before the cold.
S3.quote: I'm learning controls so I can maintain the machines, not design them.
fieldNote: Sees himself as a **maintainer** rather than a designer.
Draws on his **father's** pride in keeping things running.
Cares about **older machinists** with no degree.

steps.text: Take the first job near machines and learn every task
Study industrial controls at night school
Pay forty dollars extra on the loan each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, wait and see. A decade is long, and a lot gets promised in ten years that doesn't come true. I'd say people should plan but not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd still worry a little. Ten years gives me time to pay the loan and move toward maintenance, but I'm not fast at change. I might get stuck being comfortable until it's too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first job I can get and stay there a couple of years, saving. I'd study for a professional engineering licence, because that stays useful. I'd learn a new tool only once my supervisor says everyone has to. I'd also look at helping my dad save for a small place, since he's never owned one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, with some doubt. It's the one where I don't feel the clock ticking, and I know that can make me lazy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might get comfortable until it's too late. How would you notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When a younger person on the team starts doing things in half the time that I do the slow way. Then I'd know. I'd rather catch it myself than have my boss point it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes in your first year compared with the two-year version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could be pickier and say no to a job that leads nowhere. I could start the licence now. In the two-year version I grab anything and hold on.

say: A decade is long, and **plenty gets promised** that doesn't come true.
think: Ten years lets me pay the loan, but I'm **slow at change**.
I might get **too comfortable**, then caught out when it's too late.
do: Take the first job and **save for two years**.
Study for an **engineering licence** that stays useful.
Help **Dad** save toward a small place.
feel: **Okay with doubt**, because no clock is ticking and that can make him lazy.
S4.quote: I'd rather catch it myself than have my boss point it out.
fieldNote: Knows his own **weakness**: slowness to change.
Puts **family** ahead of career ambition by planning around his father's home.
Mood is the **lowest** of his five because a decade covers the loan.

steps.text: Stay in the first job for two years and save
Study for the professional engineering licence
Learn new tools only when the supervisor requires it
Help Dad save for a small place of his own

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because I'd have nowhere to practise before it hits. What would help is a firm that takes graduates and trains them, and a union apprenticeship list that's open. Also a slower loan schedule if I'm not working.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Nothing special. Only that I'm not asking for much. A steady job where I fix or make something is the whole plan, and I'd like to see it still exist for people like me.

headlineQuote: A steady job where I fix or make something is the whole plan
portrait: Zane is a **top mechanical engineering** graduate in Pittsburgh, four months without an offer.
He lives in his father's home in Carrick and owes **thirty-four thousand dollars** with no savings.
He never uses AI tools, prefers to **calculate by hand** and rarely blames anyone.
He leans on **practical plans**: a known supervisor, a union list, controls courses and maintenance work.
His mood is **anxious** in most worlds, alarmed at two years, and eases only slightly with a decade.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there is **no time to practise** before it hits.
whatWouldHelp: A firm that **trains graduates** and an open union apprenticeship list.
A **slower loan schedule** while he is not working.
